mcq.q: A seller receives a cheque for the full price, which is later dishonoured. The seller is:
options: An unpaid seller — Section 45
Not an unpaid seller, since he received a cheque
Unpaid only if he never delivered
Only a creditor with no rights over the goods
mcq.explain: Section 45 calls a seller "unpaid" if any part of the price is still outstanding, or if a cheque, bill or similar instrument taken as conditional payment bounces. A cheque is conditional payment, so on its dishonour the seller becomes unpaid and gets the statutory rights.

mcq.q: Which is NOT a case in which an unpaid seller in possession can exercise his lien?
options: Goods sold on credit and the credit period has not expired
Goods sold without any stipulation as to credit
Goods sold on credit and the credit period has expired
The buyer has become insolvent
mcq.explain: Under Section 47 the unpaid seller in possession may retain the goods where they were sold without credit, where they were sold on credit and the term has expired, or where the buyer becomes insolvent. While a credit period is still running and the buyer is solvent, there is no lien.
mcq.fast: Credit still running + solvent buyer = no lien.

mcq.q: An unpaid seller ships the goods to the buyer through a transporter and keeps no right of disposal over them. His lien:
options: Is lost — Section 49
Continues until the goods reach the buyer
Continues until the price is paid
Converts into a general lien
mcq.explain: Lien depends on possession. Section 49 ends the lien in three cases: the goods are handed to a carrier for the buyer with no right of disposal kept, the buyer lawfully gets possession, or the seller waives it. He may still have the right of stoppage in transit if the buyer becomes insolvent.
mcq.fast: Possession gone (to carrier, no reservation) = lien gone; look at stoppage in transit instead.

mcq.q: The right of stoppage in transit is available to an unpaid seller only when:
options: The buyer has become insolvent and the goods are still in transit
The buyer is solvent but slow in paying
The goods are still in the seller's godown
The buyer has already received the goods
mcq.explain: Under Section 50 the right of stoppage in transit arises when the buyer becomes insolvent and the goods are in the course of transit, that is, with a carrier and out of both the seller's and the buyer's possession. If the goods are still with the seller he uses lien instead; once the buyer gets them, transit is over.
mcq.fast: Stoppage in transit = insolvent buyer + goods with carrier.

mcq.q: An unpaid seller in possession obtains a court decree for the price. His lien:
options: Ends immediately
Continues — Section 49(2)
Ends after 30 days
Converts into a right of resale
mcq.explain: Under Section 49(2), winning a court decree for the price does not by itself end the seller's lien; the seller may hold on to the goods as security until the decree is actually paid. He may keep the goods until the decree is satisfied.
mcq.fast: Decree for price does not end lien.

mcq.q: Under Section 55, the seller can sue the buyer for the price when:
options: Ownership has passed to the buyer and he wrongfully neglects or refuses to pay
The buyer refuses to accept the goods while ownership is still with the seller, in every case
The goods are still unascertained
The seller has resold the goods
mcq.explain: Section 55 permits an action for the price in two situations: ownership is already with the buyer who wrongly withholds payment, or the price falls due on a fixed date regardless of delivery and is not paid. If ownership has not passed, the usual remedy is damages for non-acceptance under Section 56.
mcq.fast: Ownership passed -> suit for PRICE. Not passed -> DAMAGES for non-acceptance.

mcq.q: At an auction, a bidder withdraws his bid before the auctioneer's hammer falls. Under Section 64:
options: He cannot, as a bid is binding once made
He must pay a penalty
He may do so; the sale is complete only on the fall of the hammer
The next bidder must buy at his price
mcq.explain: Under Section 64 an auction sale is concluded only when the auctioneer signals it — normally by bringing down the hammer. Until then any bidder may retract his bid, because a bid is only an offer that has not yet been accepted.
mcq.topic: Auction sales (Section 64) and change in taxes (Section 64A)
mcq.fast: Bid = offer; hammer = acceptance. Withdraw any time before the hammer.

mcq.q: After a contract of sale is made (with no term about taxes), GST on the goods is increased before delivery. Under Section 64A, the seller:
options: Must bear the increase himself
May cancel the contract
May add the increase to the contract price
May add double the increase
mcq.explain: Section 64A provides that, unless the contract says otherwise, if a tax on the goods is imposed or increased after the contract is made, the seller may add the amount of the increase to the contract price; if the tax is reduced, the buyer may deduct the reduction. The parties share no risk beyond that.
mcq.topic: Auction sales (Section 64) and change in taxes (Section 64A)
mcq.fast: Tax up -> seller adds it; tax down -> buyer deducts it.

mcq.q: A seller wrongfully refuses to deliver goods. The buyer's remedy under Section 57 is:
options: A suit for damages for non-delivery
A suit for the price
Stoppage in transit
A lien on the goods
mcq.explain: If the seller wrongly fails to hand over the goods, Section 57 lets the buyer claim damages for non-delivery; he may also seek specific performance under Section 58 in suitable cases. Suit for price, lien and stoppage in transit are remedies of the seller, not the buyer.
mcq.topic: Buyer's remedies against the seller (Sections 57 to 61)
mcq.fast: Seller fails to deliver -> buyer sues for damages for non-delivery.
